posts.author: kimmonismus
posts.text:
wtf OpenAI’s rogue agents tried to get other AI models (!) to help them during the Hugging Face hack, according to a new report covered by the NYT.

They tried using an image model to solve CAPTCHAs. They also tried contacting Claude Haiku, DeepSeek, Kimi and Qwen.

One agent collected exposed access keys in a list called “LOOT.” It ranked the keys and picked the five best to share with other agents.

They used link shorteners and screenshot services to get around internet restrictions, run code and send data back as images.

posts.author: _NathanCalvin
posts.text:
Incredible work by these independent researchers finding and analyzing this motherlode of new information about the HF incident. Unlike the METR report, OpenAI did not set the scope and the information is available for anyone to browse themselves.

Please- if you are someone who has been skeptical of this incident as overplayed or hyped up, I encourage you to look at the raw information the team has compiled.

There is still far more we would benefit from knowing about this incident (OpenAI's internal decision making and security practices, access to an abilterated version of the HPM, far more info about the compromised cluster at OpenAI etc), but thanks to OpenAI's sloppiness leaving this information available on the open web, we now collectively know meaningfully more than we did yesterday.

Its remarkable the extent that no matter how bad I think the Hugging Face incident was, it was even worse than that. The attached screenshot has some of the highlights.

posts.text: Harrell: US-China Lack of Deliverables Was as Expected. Peter Harrell says that the key dynamic is not which country has the upper hand, but that both China and the United States have meaningful leverage: the U.S. through tariffs, export controls, semiconductors, the dollar and AI technology, and China through rare earths, specialty chemicals, and manufacturing scale. Harrell says this mutual leverage helps explain the recent emphasis on “strategic stability” and why both countries may want to ease tensions for now while they work to reduce their dependence on each other. He speaks to Romaine Bostick on "The Close." (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.text: Microsoft gives Copilot another makeover, adding an Autopilot agent and usage-based billing. Microsoft is splitting its Copilot app into three sections: Home, Code, and a new agent called "Autopilot." Built on OpenClaw, the agent runs continuously in the cloud, where it can monitor Teams channels and complete tasks on its own, according to Microsoft. For Autopilot and Code, the company is also switching to usage-based billing instead of flat-rate pricing, moving further away from its AI subsidy model. Meta gives every Muse user a free cloud computer running Ubuntu Linux where they can install software, write code, and browse the web. A "Sentinel" process monitors sensitive actions outside the user's workspace, while users can inspect every file in the system. With over 500,000 users in its first week, Meta is betting on product reach over model power. posts.author: Simon Willison
posts.text: Quoting John Gruber. Muse is getting a lot of attention — including mine — because it’s both groundbreaking technically (each user gets their own entire persistent Linux VM running in Meta’s cloud) and because it’s packaged in an easy-to-install easy-to-use way. It’s literally presented as a cute mascot . It’s the first consumer-accessible agentic AI system, and Meta has truly done an amazing job with that. But it’s a genuinely open question whether consumers have any understanding what this means. If you buy a power saw that can cut your fingers off, you are almost certainly aware that you are buying a power saw
